title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions reused the same generated candidate; the guarded pipeline could invoke repair only when the deterministic validator failed (maximum one repair call per task). Provider accounting shows 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly one repair invocation (total model calls used = 301; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Results: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR produces a materially higher pass rate (target effect 0.10 with ≈80% power) was not supported. We analyse causes (near‑ceiling baseline, minimal repair engagement), provide concrete artifact‑grounded benchmark recommendations, and list reproducibility artifacts and guidance. All preregistration, execution manifest, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived for community reuse.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and automated remediation. Prior reports show LLMs can draft configurations but commonly produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; combining generation with deterministic verification and targeted repair has been proposed to reduce misconfigurations. The community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple intent tasks, explicit validator semantics, and sealed preregistration for confirmatory evaluation of defended pipelines. To address this gap we preregistered, executed, and archived study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: a sealed experiment that (1) constructs a synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) implements a deterministic snapshot validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that enforces explicit intent constraints and required sequences, and (3) runs a paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass generator (declared model gpt-5-mini). The design intentionally used a shared‑initial generation so the baseline single‑pass output equals the guarded pipeline's initial candidate; the guarded condition could exercise at most one repair call per failed validator verdict. Our preregistered primary question: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per task), does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys document rapid growth in LLM applications for network management and enumerate challenges (hallucination, prompt injection, verification) that bear on operational deployment [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical studies show LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193, 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Tool‑assisted generate–validate–repair approaches and context‑aware prompting have shown improved correctness in focused prototypes [https://openalex.org/W4404652946]; however, these demonstrations are dataset‑ and method‑specific and typically limited in scale. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts highlight realistic risks for automated NetOps workflows and motivate guarded architectures and validator hardening [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Collectively, the literature motivates standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that (a) capture operational task structure, (b) support deterministic verification, and (c) enable confirmatory comparisons of defended architectures. Our study contributes an archived, preregistered proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a sealed confirmatory run exercising these elements.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and objectives. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution. Primary hypothesis H1: a GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration specifies task generation, validator semantics, model/configuration settings, exclusion rules, missingness treatments, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The preregistration artifact is archived (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765).

Task bank: generation, content, and constraints. A deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, and a required_sequence of field changes that must appear for a candidate to be valid. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and abstract multi‑vendor device models; all tasks are synthetic and contain no private customer data. Representative task payload fields (intent, required_sequence, difficulty label) and per‑task manifests are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097).

Validator semantics and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator performs stateless snapshot checks: it parses candidate commands, enforces the required_sequence and workflow_policies, compares the produced final_state to expected_final_state, enumerates violation codes, and returns a binary pass/fail with a diagnostic trace for each episode. The validator is intentionally conservative and deterministic to produce machine‑checkable binary outcomes suitable for confirmatory inference; per‑task scorer outputs are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json).

Experimental design: shared‑initial generation and repair budget. To isolate the incremental value of repair, each task produced one shared initial generation that served as the baseline single‑pass candidate. The guarded GVR condition validated that shared candidate and, only upon validator failure, was permitted up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This design yields a paired comparison where any guarded improvement must come from repair rather than sampling a different initial candidate. Planned_episode_count was 600 (300 shared initial + up to 300 repair calls); actual model_calls_used = 301 (accounting below).

Model and runtime configuration. The preregistered and recorded model declaration was declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" (requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") executed through the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and provider = "openai_responses". The model_configuration artifact is archived (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and records: max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. In our orchestration temperature = null combined with the hosted adapter deterministic sampling mode produced the provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Because different provider releases or invoke‑time sampling semantics change outputs, bit‑for‑bit reproduction requires replaying the archived provider traces or access to the identical provider model and settings (see Reproducibility below).

Preregistered analysis plan. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on N=300 paired binary validator outcomes. The preregistered inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Sensitivity and missingness treatments were preregistered; the run completed with no missing or excluded pairs.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. Execution completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}. The authoritative raw results file is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and the initial master prompt reference provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) are archived alongside provider traces.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is shown explicitly in Table 1 (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55; analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b).

Interpretation of the exact McNemar p and ceiling effect. The McNemar exact test focuses on discordant pairs (n10 and n01). With n10 = 1 and n01 = 0 the exact two‑sided p reported by the preregistered executor is 1.0; in practical terms this reflects that only a single discordant pair exists so there is no strong evidence of a systematic difference between conditions. The observed baseline success rate (≈0.997) makes the preregistered target detectable effect (0.10) arithmetically unattainable given the sample margins: the maximum feasible paired difference given the margins is 0.00333 (the observed value). Thus the null confirmatory outcome arises from a ceiling effect combined with minimal repair engagement rather than from analytic error.

Repair engagement and discordant episode archival. The guarded repair stage executed exactly once. The single repair invocation and its per‑episode provider call trace are archived within the raw results container execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...). Auditors wishing to examine the exact pair identifier and the standalone repair provider_call artifact should extract the relevant record from execution/raw_results.jsonl; the execution manifest and execution_raw_results index these provider traces and permit deterministic verification. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) illustrate the validator traces and difficulty labels (shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change).

Representative examples. The archived scoring JSONs include validator traces showing normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and a boolean valid flag. Example representative files (SHA‑256 listed in artifact_examples) demonstrate multi‑step workflows and show repair_applied=false for those examples; the single repair/discordant episode is present in the full raw_results artifact but is not among the representative samples printed above.

Post‑hoc power and sensitivity. The preregistered power routine targeted detection of a 0.10 paired improvement at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. Observed margins violate those assumptions: with baseline ≈0.997 the maximum detectable paired improvement is ≈0.00333. Therefore the preregistered detectable effect cannot be evaluated in this dataset and the null result is driven by arithmetic sensitivity and low repair invocation rate.
sections.discussion:
Null result scope and operational meaning. The confirmatory null pertains only to the sealed design: a deterministic synthetic task bank, a shared‑initial generation, a conservative snapshot validator, and a repair budget limited to one invocation per failed candidate. Under these constraints the guarded pipeline rarely differed from baseline (repair invoked once), so no material improvement against the preregistered target effect was possible. This outcome does not imply that GVR architectures are generically unhelpful; rather, it quantifies that when an initial generator already succeeds on nearly all tasks, localized repair with a strict trigger-and-budget policy adds negligible marginal benefit.

Concrete benchmark recommendations grounded in execution accounting. The archived artifacts support targeted design choices for future confirmatory evaluations intended to measure repair value: (A) increase task difficulty or include adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates (the execution logs show 299/300 initial successes); (B) allow iterative repair budgets per failed candidate so repair can converge (stage_counts show repair=1 indicating the budget here was inert); (C) permit multiple independent initial generations per task when the research question includes selection value rather than repair efficacy; (D) adopt stateful or emulation validators that model ordered side effects and temporal constraints to expose execution‑time failure modes; (E) include explicit adversarial prompt/test cases to exercise prompt‑injection defenses. Each recommendation maps directly to observed execution facts (300 shared generations, repair invoked only once) and to per‑task diagnostic traces archived in the bundle.

Threats to validity and scope. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baseline strategies; the observed near‑ceiling performance reduces discordance and statistical sensitivity. Construct validity: the deterministic validator enforces snapshot constraints and omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and in‑flight temporal behavior. External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstract vendors) and only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator version (v5.0) were evaluated; findings do not generalize to production networks or other models without further experiments. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant outcomes (n10=1, n01=0) leaves exploratory subgroup analysis underpowered. These threats are documented in the archived manifest and the deterministic reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Operational implications for practitioners. When generator quality is high (near‑ceiling correctness under deterministic sampling) and repair budgets are tightly constrained, guarded repair mechanisms produce minimal marginal gains. Conversely, in settings with lower generator reliability, stronger temporal validators, adversarial inputs, or relaxed repair budgets, GVR pipelines are more likely to provide measurable operational benefit. The archived artifacts permit practitioners to instantiate these harder settings without rebuilding baseline infrastructure.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported for this task set due to a ceiling effect and minimal repair engagement (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable the community to extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons to evaluate when generate–validate–repair pipelines yield measurable operational value.

Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 implemented the shared initial generation (one shared call per task) and the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline with maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation"; per‑task scorer outputs and validator traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json. Preregistered analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar and paired bootstrap CI; bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Execution accounting (authoritative): planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call). Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}. The single repair provider trace and the corresponding discordant episode are archived and indexed in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and in the execution manifest; auditors can extract the exact per‑item pair identifier and the standalone provider_call artifact by parsing those archived artifacts. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
